extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, short‑story writers, and students of fiction craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling the narrator's point of view and the broader narrative method (dramatic vs pictorial), and on matching method, pace, and techniques (scenic episodes, oblique narration, summary) to the subject of a fiction work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view governs method
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole intricate question of method ... is governed by the question of the point of view — the question of the relation in which the narrator stands to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early who is doing the seeing/telling; the narrator's relation to the story shapes whether you can be scenic, pictorial, panoramic, dramatic, or introspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize by placing the storyteller in the book
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story-teller is in the story himself ... the author is dramatized; his assertions gain in weight, for they are backed by the presence of the narrator in the pictured scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting a narrator character into the scene externalizes authority and disguises authorial arbitrariness — useful when you want the narrative claims to be seen and measured rather than merely asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show a narrator's consciousness in the moment (not only retrospect)
rubrics_metrics.description: If he is himself the subject of his story ... far better it would be to see him while his mind is actually at work in the agitation ... The matter would then be objective and visible to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the narrator's own mental state is central, prefer scenes that enact thought in real time rather than only retrospective reporting; it makes the experience more immediate and objective for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forestall the narrator — enact the action as it happens
rubrics_metrics.description: Not an account or a report ... is to be offered him, but a direct sight of the matter itself, while it is passing. Nobody expounds or explains; the story is enacted by its look and behaviour at particular moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use present enactment (scenes) when you want the reader to witness events directly; avoid explanatory narrative that distances the reader from the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject dictate the method
rubrics_metrics.description: How far he may choose to push the process ... entirely depends upon the kind of effect that the theme demands. The subject dictates the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match form to content: do not force a habitual method onto material unsuited to it. Analyze what the theme needs (intimacy, panorama, immediacy) and choose point of view and technique accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strict scenic form for purely dramatic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The purely dramatic story never deviates from a strictly scenic form ... there is no admission of the reader into the private mind of any of the characters; their thoughts and motives are transmuted into action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stories that are essentially episodes/actions, keep to observable behaviour and dialogue; this yields compactness, authority, and the modelling-like finish of drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the sacrifices of strict dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: It implies many sacrifices ... It is out of the question, of course, wherever the main burden of the story lies within some particular consciousness ... or wherever the story is too big, too comprehensive, too widely ranging, to be treated scenically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid strict scenic form when you need interiority, character growth, or a panoramic sweep; dramatization can strangle subjects requiring reflection or wide survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial (narratorial) method for wide/panoramic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: These stories, which will not naturally accommodate themselves to the reader’s point of view, and the reader’s alone, we regard as rather pictorial than dramatic — meaning that they call for some narrator, somebody who knows, to contemplate the facts and create an impression of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For comprehensive or panoramic material, employ an observing narrator (omniscient or selected) to gather and compose impressions that scenes alone cannot convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture‑making can employ dramatic techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: In picture the effect may be entrusted to the elements, the reactions of the moment, and performed by these. The mind of the narrator becomes the stage, his voice is no longer heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when using a reflective narrator, you can dramatize parts of the material by letting moments, images, and characters 'perform' the impression rather than always summarizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative summary is necessary for long spans or complex accumulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly it must be necessary to offer the reader a summary of facts, an impression of a train of events, that can only be given as somebody’s narration. Suppose it were required to render the general effect of a certain year in a man’s life ... He must narrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrated summary to compress time, convey accumulated experience, or account for what cannot be fully enacted in scenes; balance summary with select scenes to preserve vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: First person fixes point of view; third person frees time
rubrics_metrics.description: If he speaks in the first person there can, of course, be no uncertainty in the point of view ... But the author may use the man's field of vision and keep as faithfully within it as though the man were speaking for himself. In that case ... it is free in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose first person for tight spatial/experiential focus; choose third person (restricted) when you want to retain a character's viewpoint but manipulate temporal perspective (retrospect, urgency, distance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique (indirect) narration deepens vision without blurring
rubrics_metrics.description: The seeing eye is with somebody in the book, but its vision is reinforced; the picture contains more, becomes richer and fuller, because it is the author’s as well as his creature’s, both at once ... there are now two brains behind that eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use free indirect style/oblique narration to blend character perspective and authorial insight: it deepens description and thought while muting an insistently authorial voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing a congenial method onto an unsuitable subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of the book ... he simply used the method that was congenial to him, without regarding the story that he had to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-aware about your favored techniques; test whether they serve the material. A brilliant habitual method can still produce miscalculation if it fails to prepare or explain key events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condense and concentrate when the situation requires rapid constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: If, therefore, the situation is to be really made and constituted, the space it may cover must be tightly packed; the method should be that which most condenses and concentrates the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a pivotal situation must be established quickly (a turning point, a background compressed), choose methods (summary, condensed character history, panoramic rendering) that pack essential information economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small vivid scenes to create living characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If he describes how a child lingered ... the thing becomes a poetic event; in half a page he makes an unforgettable scene. The vividness of the small scene becomes a part of them ... it speeds the story by augmenting the tone and the value of the lives that we are watching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ well-observed, compact vignettes to add depth and reality to characters and to enrich the reader's impression without lengthy exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure adequate preparation before high emotional climaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to measure her passion and her resolution, because she herself is still incompletely rendered ... If she is so soon to be seen at this pitch of exaltation, it is essential that her life should be fully shared by the onlooker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not thrust a character into extreme actions or crises before the reader has enough of their internal life and circumstances to judge the motives; otherwise actions feel arbitrary or unimportant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep method consistent with the demands of clarity and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The first part of the book is neither one thing nor the other; it is not an independent drama ... and on the other hand it is not a sufficient preparation for the great picture of inevitable disaster which is to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unclear mixes of scenic and pictorial treatment that leave early sections underdeveloped or fail to prepare later consequences; structure choices should serve clarity and cumulative effect.
